title: Electrical Installation
summary: Learn the essentials of building wiring: safety, safe isolation and the law, the supply and distribution board, circuits and load calculations, cable sizing and voltage drop, earthing, protection and testing, and fault finding and solar backup. Calculations were checked in code; always follow your national wiring code.
audience: Apprentice electricians, technicians, property managers and DIY learners who want to understand wiring safely

body.p: Electrical installation work covers wiring buildings for lighting, sockets, appliances, motors and solar systems. Poor work causes fires, electric shocks and deaths, so it is controlled by law and wiring codes, such as SANS 10142 in South Africa and codes based on IEC or BS 7671 rules in many other countries. In most countries only registered or licensed electricians may do installation work and issue certificates of compliance.

steps: Identify the circuit to be worked on.
Switch off and isolate it at the distribution board.
Lock off the isolator and attach a warning tag.
Prove your voltage tester works on a known live source.
Test that the circuit is dead between all conductors.
Re-prove the tester, then start work.

list: Electric shock: current through the body can stop the heart.
Burns and arc flash from short circuits.
Fire from overloaded or loose connections.
Falls from ladders while working at height.

body.tip: Never work live to save time. A few minutes isolating a circuit can save a life.

body.p: Mains supply arrives from the utility through a service cable to the meter (often a prepaid meter) and then to the distribution board (DB), where it is split into circuits.

list: Main switch: isolates the whole installation.
Earth-leakage unit or residual current device (RCD): trips when current leaks to earth, typically set at 30 mA to protect people from shock.
Circuit breakers (miniature circuit breakers, MCBs): protect each circuit's cables from overload and short circuit.
Surge protection: guards electronics from lightning and switching surges.
Earth bar and neutral bar, kept separate and clearly labelled.

body.p: Colour codes vary by country and age of installation. A common modern single-phase scheme is brown for live (phase), blue for neutral and green/yellow for earth; older installations may use red, black and green. Always confirm with testing, never by colour alone.

body.tip: Label every circuit breaker clearly, for example "Kitchen sockets" or "Geyser", so anyone can isolate the right one quickly.

body.p: An installation is divided into separate circuits for lighting, socket outlets, and large fixed appliances such as stoves, geysers (water heaters) and air conditioners. Separating them limits the effect of a fault and stops one circuit carrying too much current.

For single-phase loads, I = P / V. A 3000 W kettle at 230 V draws 3000 / 230 = 13.04 A. A lighting circuit with six 100 W loads and two 60 W loads totals 720 W, or about 3.13 A. A socket circuit expected to run a 2000 W heater, a 1500 W iron and an 800 W microwave at once would draw 4300 / 230, about 18.7 A, near the limit of a 20 A circuit.

list: Lighting circuits commonly use 1.5 mm² cable and 10 A breakers.
Socket circuits commonly use 2.5 mm² cable with 16 or 20 A breakers.
Stoves and geysers have dedicated circuits with larger cables.
Breaker rating must not exceed what the cable can safely carry.

body.tip: Check your local code tables; cable ratings depend on installation method, grouping and temperature.

lessons.title: Cables, voltage drop and installation methods

body.p: Cables are chosen for current-carrying capacity, voltage drop, the environment and mechanical protection.

Long cable runs lose voltage. Tables give the drop in millivolts per amp per metre (mV/A/m). For a cable rated at 18 mV/A/m carrying 20 A over 25 m, the drop is 18 x 20 x 25 / 1000 = 9 V, which is 9 / 230 = 3.9% of the supply. Many codes allow up to about 5% (11.5 V on 230 V); if the run were longer, a thicker cable would be needed.

list: Conduit (PVC or steel) protects single-core cables in walls and ceilings.
Surface trunking is used where walls cannot be chased.
Armoured cables are used underground and outdoors; bury them at the required depth with warning tape.
Terminations must be tight: loose connections overheat and cause fires.
Keep power cables apart from data and telephone cables.

body.tip: Measure the actual route length, including drops down walls, before choosing a cable size.

body.p: Earthing connects exposed metal parts (appliance cases, metal pipes, DB enclosures) to earth, so if a live wire touches them, a large fault current flows and the protective device trips quickly. Without good earthing, the metal could stay live and kill someone who touches it.

list: An earth electrode (earth spike) or the supplier's earth provides the connection.
Bonding links metal water and gas pipes and other metalwork to the main earth.
Earth-leakage units protect against shocks even when earthing is imperfect, but they are not a replacement for it.
Visual inspection of workmanship, labelling and correct breakers.
Continuity of earth conductors.
Insulation resistance between conductors, using an insulation tester (often at 500 V DC); values should be very high, typically in megohms.
Polarity: switches and breakers in the live conductor.
Earth loop impedance and earth-leakage trip tests.

body.p: Results are recorded on a test report and certificate of compliance.

body.tip: Press the test button on earth-leakage units regularly; if it does not trip, call an electrician.

steps: Ask what happened and when: what was switched on, did it trip at once or later?
Check which breaker or earth-leakage unit tripped.
Unplug appliances on that circuit and reset; an appliance fault often causes earth-leakage trips.
Isolate and test the circuit for insulation faults if tripping continues.
Look for damaged cables, water in fittings and loose terminals.

body.p: Inverters, batteries and solar panels are now common in homes and businesses. They must be installed to code with correct DC isolators, fuses, earthing and a changeover arrangement so they never feed power back into the grid during an outage, which could kill line workers.

Electricians train through trade colleges, apprenticeships and trade tests, then register with the national authority. Opportunities include domestic and industrial installation, maintenance, solar installation and running your own business.

body.tip: Keep up with code changes and product updates; standards are revised regularly.

quiz.q: Before working on a circuit you should:
options: Isolate, lock off and prove it dead

quiz.q: A residual current device protects people by tripping at about:

options: Cables from overload and short circuit

quiz.q: A 3000 W kettle at 230 V draws about:
Six 100 W and two 60 W lights total:
18 mV/A/m, 20 A, 25 m gives a voltage drop of:
9 V drop on 230 V is about:
Loose terminations are dangerous because they:

options: Causes a large current that trips protection quickly
An insulation tester at a high DC voltage

quiz.q: A frequent cause of earth-leakage tripping is:

options: Feed power back into the grid during an outage
